newsitem.title: USA: Bond lwyrs question senator's yield burning plan.
newsitem.headline: Bond lwyrs question senator's yield burning plan.

text.p: A representative of bond lawyers warned that the 1986 False Claims Act, which a top U.S. senator will urge the U.S. Justice Department on Friday to use to crack down on alleged "yield burning," may not be a viable solution.
The 11-year-old law permits Justice to take action against any party that causes financial loss to the U.S. Treasury. Justice can seek treble damages and penalties.
But Amy Dunbar, director of government affairs for the National Association of Bond Lawyers, said there could be problems because the law does not cover "tax cases."

"Tax cases are specifically prohibited under the law," she said. "In other words, you can't call up and say I know my neighbor hasn't been paying his taxes for the past three years and, so, I want to file for treble damages."

Sen. Charles Grassley, R-Iowa, a top member of the Senate Finance and Judiciary Committees, is expected to send letters to Justice and the Internal Revenue Service on January 31 urging the agencies to tap provisions of the 1986 law to resolve yield burning, a knowledgeable source told Reuters.

The $1.3 trillion dollar municipal bond market has been rocked by recent charges that bond underwriters overbill issuers for U.S. Treasuries bought in the open market and used in bond financing transactions, a practice dubbed yield burning.

Grassley's strategy, if successful, could take the pressure off off muni bond issuers who are being asked by Treasury to pay off yield burning debts even though most had no knowledge that their dealers may have engaged in the practice, the source said.

IRS notified issuers last year that they can avoid having interest on their bonds declared taxable by IRS if they pay Treasury the difference between the price they paid and the spot price of the securities on the purchase date, plus interest. Issuers are uniformly opposed to the plan.
PSA The Bond Market Trade Association had no comment on the upcoming letters to Justice and IRS.
